beats.headline: Static variables do not reside in Metaspace.
beats.subline: Stop repeating the myth. Here is where your static fields actually sit.
beats.narration: You have heard static variables sit in Metaspace. That is wrong. In modern HotSpot, class metadata lives in Metaspace, but the actual static field values reside on the Java Heap.

beats.title: Where Static Data Resides
beats.subtitle: Metaspace vs. Heap

nodes.label: Metaspace
nodes.detail: Stores InstanceKlass, bytecode, and method tables.

nodes.label: Static Fields
nodes.detail: Stored inside the Class mirror object on the Heap.

beats.narration: Metaspace holds the class structure, but the static fields themselves reside inside the java dot lang dot Class mirror object on the Heap. This makes them permanent GC roots.

beats.title: The Static Memory Leak

steps.explanation: Because it is static, the ClassLoader keeps this map alive forever.
Unbounded static collections will eventually trigger OutOfMemoryError.

beats.narration: Because static fields are GC roots, they stay alive as long as the ClassLoader exists. An unbounded static map is a classic recipe for a memory leak.

beats.title: Access Patterns

top.label: Bad Practice
points: Hides that it is a static call

beats.narration: Never access static members through an object instance. It compiles, but it is misleading. Always use the class name to signal that no instance is involved.

beats.title: Part 1 Summary
takeaways: Static fields reside on the Heap
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Why static methods cannot override →
beats.narration: Static fields are powerful but dangerous. In Part 2, we look at why static methods do not support polymorphism and how to build clean utility classes.

beats.headline: You cannot override a static method.
beats.subline: Attempting to do so triggers Method Hiding—a silent logic trap.
beats.narration: If you try to override a static method, the compiler will not stop you, but you will be hiding it instead. This creates massive bugs in polymorphic code.

beats.title: Method Hiding vs Overriding

steps.explanation: Static methods use invokestatic, which binds at compile time.
It prints Base because the reference type is Base.

beats.narration: Because static methods use invokestatic, they bind to the declared reference type, not the runtime object. This is why you should never treat them like instance methods.

beats.title: The Utility Class Pattern
beats.narration: For pure utility classes, make the class final and add a private constructor that throws an error. This enforces the static-only design pattern.

beats.title: Bytecode Dispatch
beats.caption: Static vs Instance calls
beats.narration: Check the bytecode. invokestatic is a direct jump to the class method. invokevirtual performs a lookup based on the object's runtime class.

beats.title: Part 2 Summary
takeaways: Static methods are hidden, not overridden
Use final + private ctor for utilities

beats.narration: Static methods are for pure logic, not polymorphism. In Part 3, we dive into static initialization blocks and how they can accidentally deadlock your JVM.

beats.headline: Your static block could deadlock your app.
beats.subline: The JVM locks classes during initialization. Here is the circular dependency trap.
beats.narration: Static blocks are thread-safe, but that safety comes with a price. If you have circular dependencies in your static initializers, you will deadlock the JVM.

beats.title: The Deadlock Sequence
beats.subtitle: Circular Dependency Trap

nodes.label: Deadlock
nodes.detail: A needs B, B needs A

beats.narration: The JVM holds a lock while running the static initializer. If Class A waits for Class B, and B waits for A, you are stuck in a permanent deadlock.

beats.title: Static Init Block

steps.explanation: The JVM compiles this into a special method called clinit.
The JVM ensures this block runs at most once.

beats.narration: The JVM compiles static blocks into a clinit method. It is lazy and thread-safe, but keep the logic simple to avoid poisoning the class with errors.

beats.title: Bill Pugh Singleton

steps.explanation: Holder is only loaded when get() is called.

beats.narration: Use the Holder idiom for lazy singletons. It relies on the JVM's class initialization guarantees to provide thread safety without any explicit synchronization.

beats.title: Part 3 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Why main must be static →
beats.narration: Static blocks are powerful for one-time setup. In Part 4, we wrap up by explaining why the main method requires the static keyword.

beats.headline: Why does main() have to be static?
beats.subline: It is not just a convention. It solves a fundamental startup paradox.
beats.narration: Why is the main method static? Because when the JVM starts, no objects exist yet. If main were not static, the JVM would not know how to create your app.

beats.title: The Startup Paradox
beats.subtitle: Why static is mandatory

nodes.label: JVM Launch
nodes.detail: Class is loaded, but no instances exist.

beats.narration: If main were an instance method, the JVM would need to guess which constructor to call. Static main avoids this ambiguity entirely.

beats.title: The Signature Explained

steps.explanation: JVM does not use the return value.

beats.narration: Public for access, static for startup, void because the JVM does not care about the return value. It is the perfect contract for an entry point.

beats.title: Modern Entry Points
beats.narration: Java 25 simplified this for scripts, but for production, the static main remains the standard. It is the backbone of every Java app.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Static fields are Heap-based GC roots
Use static for pure utilities only
